Ye
yē
pron. (second person plural, nominative; rendering Hebrew 'attem, Greek humeis)
From Saxon ge, the plural of þu. In the Authorized Version ye is the plural nominative and you the plural objective, exactly parallel to thou and thee in the singular. The four-way system is complete and the translators keep it.

Biblical Definition

Ye is the second person plural — more than one person addressed together — and it is the pronoun of the congregation, the covenant people, and the church. Where thou isolates, ye gathers. The serpent uses it to make the prohibition sound collective and therefore negotiable: “Ye shall not eat of it, neither shall ye touch it, lest ye die” (Genesis 3:3). Christ uses it to lay a single condition on all His hearers at once: “Except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 18:3). Peter's sifting is the classic case of the two pronouns working together — Satan desired to have you, plural, all the apostles, but the Lord says “I have prayed for thee”, singular, for Peter alone. An English Bible that renders both as you makes that exchange invisible. The plural is not a lesser word than the singular. It is how Scripture addresses a people, and losing it costs the reader every place where a promise or a warning is corporate rather than individual.

Webster 1828 Definition

The nominative plural of the second person; the pronoun by which more than one person is addressed. In Scripture it is the pronoun of the assembled people — the congregation warned, the disciples commissioned, the church exhorted together.

expand to see more

YE, pron. [Sax. ge.] The nominative case of the second person plural; the plural of thou.

2. It is properly distinguished from you, which is the objective case; ye do, but I see you.

3. In common modern usage the distinction is lost, and you serves for both cases and both numbers.

4. It is retained in the solemn style and throughout the common version of the Scriptures.

5. In Scripture, Except ye be converted, Matt. 18; Ye shall not eat of it, Gen. 3.

Key Scripture

Genesis 3:3 — "But of the fruit of the tree which is in the midst of the garden, God hath said, Ye shall not eat of it, neither shall ye touch it, lest ye die."

Matthew 18:3 — "And said, Verily I say unto you, Except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven."

Psalm 2:12 — "Kiss the Son, lest he be angry, and ye perish from the way, when his wrath is kindled but a little. Blessed are all they that put their trust in him."

John 5:33 — "Ye sent unto John, and he bare witness unto the truth."

Modern Corruption

The collapse of ye into you hides every corporate address in Scripture, and it feeds a real error: the reading of promises made to the church as though they were made to the private individual, and of warnings given to a congregation as though they were meant for someone else in it.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle needing recovery is the corporate address of Scripture. A great many of the New Testament's most quoted assurances are plural: they are spoken to a church, and they are kept toward a church. Read as private guarantees to the individual believer they are made to promise things they never promised, and the reader is then disappointed by God for a debt God never contracted. The plural pronoun is a guard against that, and it is the first casualty of a translation that flattens the number.

The error runs in the other direction too. When a warning addressed to the whole assembly is heard as you in the vague modern sense, every hearer may quietly assign it to his neighbour. The apostolic letters are largely written to congregations, and their rebukes are congregational; the church that reads them corporately must repent corporately. Recovering the distinction is not antiquarianism. It is the difference between hearing Scripture as it was dictated and hearing a blurred version of it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew 'attem (masculine plural) and 'atten (feminine plural); Greek humeis, the plural nominative, with humas and humin for the oblique cases; Saxon ge, the ancestor of ye.

expand to see more

Hebrew 'attem (H859) — ye, masculine plural; the address to Israel assembled at Sinai and at Shechem.

Hebrew 'atten (H859) — ye, feminine plural; rarer, used of the women of Israel and of the cities.

Greek humeis (G5210) — ye, nominative plural; emphatic when written out, as in ye are the salt of the earth.

Greek humas (G5209) — you, accusative plural; the form behind Satan's desire to have you in Luke 22:31.

Saxon ge — the Old English plural nominative; the Authorized Version keeps ye nominative and you objective throughout.

Usage

"Of the serpent making a singular prohibition sound collective: Ye shall not eat of it, neither shall ye touch it (Genesis 3:3)."

"Of one condition laid upon all hearers at once: Except ye be converted, and become as little children (Matthew 18:3)."

"Of a warning to the whole congregation: Kiss the Son, lest he be angry, and ye perish from the way (Psalm 2:12)."
